records.sourceFile: Exploring the interplay between metabolic power and equivalent distance in training games and official matches in soccer - A machine learning approach.pdf

paper.citation: Manzi V, Savoia C, Padua E, Edriss S, Iellamo F, Caminiti G, et al. Exploring the interplay between metabolic power and equivalent distance in training games and official matches in soccer: a machine learning approach. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1230912.
paper.abstract: In 21 elite male Serie A players over one season, four machine learning classifiers separated training games from official matches using metabolic power and equivalent distance index, although overall external load intensity did not differ between the two. Training load calculated from metabolic power metrics correlated with Edwards' heart-rate-based training load (individual r = 0.59 to 0.87). The authors conclude that these metrics can indicate differences between the two session types.
paper.tldr: Metabolic power and equivalent distance index separated training games from official matches in one elite soccer squad even though overall intensity was similar, and load built from these metrics tracked Edwards' heart-rate load. Because games and matches were measured with different tracking systems and training games made up most of the data, the classification result is a weak basis for redesigning training games.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of 4,269 training games and 380 official matches from 21 elite male players in Serie A over the 2021-2022 season; training was tracked with GPEXE 18-Hz GPS and matches with the STATS SportVU multicamera system. Metabolic power and equivalent distance index were used to build KNN, decision tree, random forest and SVM classifiers with 3-fold stratified cross-validation, and Pearson correlations compared Edwards' training load with metabolic-power-based load.
paper.findings: The four classifiers discriminated training games from matches, with AUC of 0.89 to 0.98 and classification accuracy of 0.93 to 0.98 across playing positions in Table 2. There was no significant difference in overall intensity between training games and matches (mean difference 0.01 AU), and metabolic-power-based training load correlated with Edwards' training load at r = 0.59 to 0.87 within players and r = 0.75 for the team (p < 0.001). Metabolic power and equivalent distance index were not significantly correlated with each other (r = 0.017), and area per player was not correlated with training-game intensity.
paper.limitations: The sample is a retrospective convenience sample from one squad, and the authors state the study should be read as a case study. Training games came from GPS and matches from optical tracking, and with 4,269 training games against 380 matches a classifier that always predicted 'training game' would already be about 92% accurate, so the reported accuracy is less informative than it appears; the paper does not report metabolic power or equivalent distance values for each session type. The abstract and Results give AUC of 0.90 to 0.96 and accuracy of 0.89 to 0.98, while Table 2 gives AUC of 0.89 to 0.98 and accuracy of 0.93 to 0.98, and the cross-validation description does not state whether folds were split by player.
paper.practicalImplications: Metabolic-power-based training load tracked heart-rate training load within players in this squad, which supports its use as one external load measure alongside others. The claim that training games differ from matches in how intensity is produced rests on a classifier that may reflect different tracking systems and class imbalance, so it should not drive training-game design on its own. The authors' suggestion to copy exact percentages of high-speed metabolic power was not tested in this study.
paper.athleteDev: Staff using GPS metabolic power can expect it to track heart-rate training load reasonably well within individual players (r = 0.59 to 0.87 in this squad). Whether training games reproduce how match intensity is produced is not settled by this study, because the paper does not report the session-type values and the classification may be confounded by measurement system.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It analyzes training and match load in a squad and does not assess injury, rehabilitation or readiness after injury.

paper.citation: Junge N, Lundsgaard A, Hansen MF, Samozino P, Morin JB, Aagaard P, et al. Force-velocity-power profiling of maximal effort sprinting, jumping and hip thrusting: Exploring the importance of force orientation specificity for assessing neuromuscular function. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2021.
paper.abstract: The authors compared force-velocity-power (FVP) profiles from maximal sprint acceleration, squat jump and hip thrust in 41 professional male footballers. They tested whether the profiles are linked across these tasks, to judge whether hip thrust profiling reflects sprint-specific neuromuscular function.
paper.tldr: In elite footballers, maximal power (Pmax) was shared between sprinting and squat jumping, but the force and velocity components were not. Hip thrust Pmax was not related to sprint Pmax, so hip thrust profiling should not be read as a direct measure of sprint profile.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional correlational design in 41 male professional footballers from two Danish Super League teams. Sprint FVP was derived from three 30 m sprints timed with photocells (time-shift method); squat jump FVP from unloaded and loaded jumps (+30 and +60 kg); hip thrust FVP from five loads (+40 to +120 kg) with high-frequency video. Pearson correlations were calculated between matching F0, V0, Pmax and SFv across tasks, with n = 26, 29 and 32 for the paired comparisons.
paper.findings: Sprint and squat jump Pmax were correlated (r = 0.73, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.87, P < 0.001; n = 26). Squat jump and hip thrust Pmax were correlated (r = 0.44, P = 0.01; n = 32). Sprint and hip thrust Pmax were not correlated (r = 0.18, P = 0.36; n = 29). No significant correlations were found for F0, V0 or SFv between any two tasks (r between -0.19 and 0.20). The authors report that these findings are consistent with task specificity in neuromuscular function.
paper.limitations: Sprint profiles were computed from split times and the hip thrust from video, and the authors note that the validity of the hip thrust FVP is not well established. Sub-sample sizes differ across the three comparisons (n = 26 to 32) because of player transfers and minor injuries. The population was a homogeneous group of male professional footballers, so the findings may not generalise to other sports, sexes or training levels.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who profile footballers should not assume that a hip thrust FVP profile reflects sprint acceleration capacity, since Pmax was not related between these two tasks in this group. Squat jump and sprint Pmax were moderately correlated (r = 0.73, n = 26), but F0 and V0 were not, so one test cannot substitute for the other when force or velocity capacity is the question.
paper.athleteDev: Profiling the hip thrust separately from sprinting and jumping may give extra information on individual neuromuscular constraints. The study does not show that hip thrust training improves sprint capacity, and the authors state that transfer from hip thrust to sprint-specific function may be limited in high-level players.
paper.rtp: This study does not address injury or return to sport. Its participants were free of injury at testing, so the findings cannot be used to judge recovery of sprint or jump capacity after injury.

records.sourceFile: From data to action - A scoping review of wearable technologies and biomechanical assessments informing injury prevention strategies in sport.pdf

paper.citation: Rebelo A, Martinho DV, Valente-dos-Santos J, Coelho-e-Silva MJ, Teixeira DS. From data to action: a scoping review of wearable technologies and biomechanical assessments informing injury prevention strategies in sport. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2023;15:169.
paper.abstract: This scoping review maps 21 studies on wearable and biomechanical technologies used in athletes to inform training adaptation and injury prevention. The authors searched PubMed/Medline, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science to June 2023, following PRISMA-ScR. They report that Player Load, change-of-direction measures and the acute:chronic workload ratio were the most used metrics for injury-related decisions, and that force plates helped assess fatigue and rehabilitation.
paper.tldr: GPS, accelerometers and force plates are widely used in sport, and Player Load is the most common metric. The authors see these tools as useful for individualizing loads and assessing fatigue, but they note that device validity and reliability are reported in fewer than half of the studies.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with a protocol registered on the Open Science Framework (June 2023). The authors searched PubMed/Medline, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science (last run June 15, 2023), limited results to English-language journal articles, and had each source charted by at least two reviewers. A basic quality check was done during charting but did not affect inclusion, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed.
paper.findings: Of 735 records, 21 studies were included: 10 in male athletes only, 8 in female athletes only, and 3 in both sexes. One cited American football study reported that a greater proportion of injuries occurred at an acute:chronic workload ratio above 1.6, and force plate studies in female volleyball, handball and basketball examined biomechanical variables linked to ACL injury risk. The authors describe these as mapped findings, not pooled conclusions about injury prediction.
paper.limitations: No formal risk-of-bias assessment was done, so study quality was not critically appraised, and the review says it may have missed newer or less frequently studied technologies. Only 9 of 21 studies (43%) reported device validity or reliability, and the authors note that device heterogeneity limits comparison. The search was limited to English-language journal articles.
paper.practicalImplications: Monitor Player Load and acute:chronic workload alongside position-specific drill demands, as the included soccer, volleyball and American football studies did. Confirm a device's validity and reliability before using it for decisions, because fewer than half of the included studies reported these. Use force plate jump and landing tests to track mechanics over time, as several studies did, rather than as stand-alone injury predictors.
paper.athleteDev: Use GPS and accelerometer data to compare positional and drill demands and to set individual loads, as several included studies did. Pair device data with athlete-reported and performance measures, because the authors note that privacy concerns, discomfort and limited data-interpretation skills can reduce uptake.
paper.rtp: The review cites rehabilitation uses, such as force plate tests during hamstring and ankle rehabilitation and workload management during recovery in professional soccer. These come from individual studies, and the review sets no pass criteria, so the findings cannot be used as return-to-play clearance standards.

records.sourceFile: GPS derived workload metrics and injury risk in team-based field sports - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Kupperman N, Hertel J. Global Positioning System-Derived Workload Metrics and Injury Risk in Team-Based Field Sports: A Systematic Review. J Athl Train. 2020;55(9).
paper.abstract: This systematic review of PubMed studies from January 2009 to May 2019 evaluated whether GPS-derived workload metrics are associated with musculoskeletal injury risk in team-based field-sport athletes. Total distance, high-speed running and acute:chronic workload ratios were the most common metrics. Many metrics were associated with injury in individual studies, but the authors concluded the evidence was inconclusive for any metric across sports.
paper.tldr: Workload metrics such as total distance, high-speed running and acute:chronic workload ratios were linked to injury in some individual studies, but no metric predicted injury consistently across sports. Treat these metrics as descriptive associations until injury definitions and methods are standardised.
paper.methods: Systematic review of PubMed records (January 2009 to May 2019) using search terms for GPS, workload, injury and team field sports. Eligible studies were original research that used GPS-derived variables as predictors and injury as the main outcome in team field-sport athletes only. Two independent raters graded study quality with the NIH observational-study tool, and a meta-analysis was not possible because of heterogeneity.
paper.findings: Across 22 studies, results for the same metric often conflicted. For example, high one-week total distance was linked to higher injury risk in some studies and to lower risk in others. Acute:chronic workload ratios above about 2.0 were associated with higher injury risk in several studies, but these findings used different ratio methods and varied in strength, and five studies relied on magnitude-based inference, which the review describes as mathematically refuted.
paper.limitations: The review could not pool results, and most included studies covered one team over one season. None of the included studies involved female athletes, and the authors note that none came close to the sample sizes needed for the number of predictors modelled. The per-sport counts in the text (10 Australian football, 6 soccer, 5 rugby, 1 Gaelic, 1 American football) add to 23 for 22 studies and do not match Table 2 (9 Australian football), and some in-text study citations appear misnumbered.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use a single GPS workload metric or acute:chronic ratio threshold to predict injury in an individual athlete, because the authors say unvalidated models offer descriptive associations, not prediction. Record injury definitions and load thresholds consistently so results can be compared. The authors recommend a four-tier daily availability classification that captures partial participation, which binary time-loss injury records miss.
paper.athleteDev: Use GPS workload data to describe training and match loads, not as validated targets for performance. Avoid applying one squad's cut-offs as universal load limits, since the review found that the thresholds did not transfer consistently across teams.
paper.rtp: This review studies injury risk in athletes who were participating in team sport and does not evaluate return to sport or rehabilitation. Its findings cannot be used to set return-to-play decisions or GPS-based rehabilitation loads.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring to quadriceps fatigue      ratio offers new and different muscle function information than the      conventional non-fatigued ratio.pdf

paper.citation: Pinto MD, Blazevich AJ, Andersen LL, Mil-Homens P, Pinto RS. Hamstring-to-quadriceps fatigue ratio offers new and different muscle function information than the conventional non-fatigued ratio. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2017.
paper.abstract: Thirty-five professional soccer players completed a 30-repetition isokinetic knee extension and flexion fatigue test. The conventional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio was calculated for the non-fatigued state and in fatigue, and several fatigue index methods were compared. Knee flexor and extensor moments fell significantly by the sixth repetition, and fatigue-state ratios were significantly higher than the conventional ratio but only weakly correlated with it. The authors suggest the fatigue ratio gives different information and needs prospective testing for injury prediction.
paper.tldr: A hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio taken during fatigue gave larger values that were only weakly related to the usual non-fatigued ratio. It is a new measure that has not been shown to predict injury or return to sport.
paper.methods: Thirty-five professional soccer players performed 30 continuous concentric knee extension and flexion repetitions at 300 deg/s on a Cybex Norm dynamometer in preseason. Conventional and fatigue-state hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios were calculated, along with fatigue indices using several published and new methods. Relationships were tested with Pearson and Spearman correlations and paired comparisons with effect sizes.
paper.findings: Knee extensor and flexor moments were significantly reduced by the sixth repetition and fell further to the end. The fatigue-state ratios were 1.25-1.38 compared with 0.70 for the conventional ratio (p<.01 for repetitions 28 and 30; repetition 29 was not significant but had a large effect size). The conventional ratio correlated weakly with the repetition-30 fatigue ratio (r=.39, p=.02) and not significantly with the repetition 28 and 29 ratios (rs=0.25-0.27), so player rankings differed. The decline in the conventional ratio was strongly correlated with knee flexor fatigue in repetitions 28-30 (r=.80-.84).
paper.limitations: Reliability was not measured, because players had limited time for laboratory visits in preseason. Eccentric hamstring strength was not tested. The authors note that the fatigue index method and angular velocity affect the results, and the test is untested as a predictor of injury or return to sport.
paper.practicalImplications: A fatigue-state ratio calculated from a 30-repetition isokinetic test gives different values and different player rankings from the conventional ratio, so the two should not be used interchangeably. Staff should not treat the fatigue ratio as an injury-risk threshold until prospective data exist.
paper.athleteDev: The paper suggests knee flexor fatigue may explain changes in the conventional ratio more than knee extensor fatigue. Staff could use this to guide fatigue-resistance work for the hamstrings, but the study did not test training effects.
paper.rtp: The fatigue ratio has not been shown to inform return to sport. The authors suggest it may help return-to-sport decisions in future studies, but this study had no injured players and no return-to-sport outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Heart rate variability activity in soccer athletes after a musculoskeletal injury.pdf

paper.citation: Flores G, Monteiro D, Silva F, Duarte-Mendes P. Heart rate variability activity in soccer athletes after a musculoskeletal injury. J Rehabil Med. 2024;56:jrm24969.
paper.abstract: This study measured heart rate variability (HRV) in 15 semi-professional male soccer players within 72 hours of a musculoskeletal injury and again 5 to 7 days after full return to play. Low-frequency power and the LF/HF ratio were lower after injury, and high-frequency power was higher. The authors conclude that HRV may help detect autonomic imbalance and support safer return to play, and they call for controlled studies and baseline values.
paper.tldr: In 15 injured semi-professional soccer players, HRV measured within 72 hours of injury differed from HRV measured after return to play, with lower LF power and LF/HF ratio and higher normalized HF power soon after injury. With no control group or pre-injury baseline, this is a within-group change only.
paper.methods: Longitudinal study of 15 male semi-professional soccer players with a recent musculoskeletal injury, from three clubs in central Portugal; one further athlete was excluded as a statistical outlier. After 5 minutes seated rest, HRV was recorded standing for 8 minutes with a Polar H10 strap and m200 watch, and minutes 2 to 8 were analysed in the frequency domain at T1 (within 72 hours of injury) and T2 (5 to 7 days after full return to play). Paired t-tests or Wilcoxon tests were used, with an a priori power analysis requiring n = 15.
paper.findings: At T1 compared with T2, LF power (n.u.) was lower (69.5 vs 83.7, p = 0.001), HF power (n.u.) was higher (30.5 vs 16.3, p = 0.001) and the LF/HF ratio was lower (median 2.81 vs 5.42, p = 0.001). HF power in ms2 differed between time points (p = 0.017), although the reported medians were similar (205 vs 218 ms2), and LF power in ms2 did not differ (p = 0.233).
paper.limitations: No control group or pre-injury baseline, injuries of nine types including traumatic ones, and 6 athletes with a prior similar injury; stress and pain were not controlled. One athlete was excluded as a statistical outlier, but the number recruited is not reported in the text (the abstract says 15 were recruited). The higher HF power after injury conflicts with earlier studies, which the authors note were mostly in concussion, and the abstract's 'high values after injury' for HF power does not match the ms2 medians in Table II.
paper.practicalImplications: HRV could be explored as one monitoring signal during recovery from musculoskeletal injury, alongside clinical assessment. The study suggests individual pre-injury baseline values would be needed before a post-injury change could be interpreted.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable to training prescription. The study measures autonomic changes after injury and does not test training or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The study compares HRV in the acute phase with HRV after full return to play, and the authors suggest it could help identify a safer return. It does not test return-to-play decisions or show that HRV predicts re-injury, so it cannot set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Heat Stroke Burden and Validity of Wearable Derived Core Temperature Estimation during Elite Military Training.pdf

paper.citation: Hintz C, Presley DM, Butler CR. Heat Stroke Burden and Validity of Wearable-Derived Core Temperature Estimation during Elite Military Training. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: A retrospective case series and device validity study of exertional heat stroke among elite Air Force Special Warfare trainees wearing a Zephyr Bioharness. Of 10 confirmed heat stroke cases, 8 had estimated core temperature below the 39.7 C alert threshold, giving 20% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity. The authors conclude that the device had substantial false-positive and false-negative rates and should be used with extreme caution.
paper.tldr: In elite military trainees, a chest-strap estimate of core temperature missed 8 of 10 confirmed heat stroke cases and produced 499 alerts, only 2 of which were heat stroke. The authors say medical staff, not the device, should be the first line of detection.
paper.methods: Retrospective study of 1,364 trainees whose estimated core temperature was monitored in real time during strength and conditioning, running and rucking from January to September 2021, with peak ECT recorded per session. Trainees reaching 39.7 C stopped and were assessed; those with CNS dysfunction had rectal temperature measured, and heat stroke was diagnosed by an on-site physician and treated with cold water immersion. Incidence, sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios and Bland-Altman limits of agreement for the 10 cases were calculated in R.
paper.findings: Of 47,058 daily peak ECT readings, 499 (1.1%) were flagged above 39.7 C, and only 2 of the flagged trainees had confirmed heat stroke. Ten heat stroke cases were confirmed (0.8 per 1,000 person-months), with peak rectal temperatures of 39.4 to 42.2 C and peak ECT of 37.8 to 40.6 C; sensitivity was 20%, specificity 98.9%, positive likelihood ratio 18.93 and negative likelihood ratio 0.81. The Bland-Altman plot showed low agreement between ECT and rectal temperature.
paper.limitations: Retrospective design with only 10 cases, one of them a recurrence in the same trainee, and no reference temperature for trainees without CNS signs. The paper is inconsistent on sex: the abstract and Table 2 report 9 men and 1 woman, while the Results describe the cases as 100% male, and the Results call the trainees athletes. The abstract describes 499 flagged trainees, while the Results describe 499 flagged measurements, and the Bland-Altman bias and limits are shown only in a figure.
paper.practicalImplications: This device's core temperature alert should not be relied on to detect heat stroke, because most cases occurred below the alert threshold. The authors recommend that medical staff on site remain the first line of detection, with rectal temperature and CNS assessment to confirm suspected cases, and they note that reviewing frequent false alerts takes staff time.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable to training prescription. The study does not test performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to activity after heat stroke. Table 2 lists a gradual return to training for all 10 cases, but the protocol is not described.
